title: KoBold Metals used an AI drilling planner to appraise the Mingomba copper deposit in Zambia
summary: KoBold Metals used the Intelligent Prospector drilling planner to help appraise the high-grade zone of the Mingomba copper deposit in about eight months; no source isolates the effect of AI.
source_collection: University of Texas AI Opportunity Inventory
account: Jef Caers of Stanford University co-developed the Intelligent Prospector drilling planner. His 2023 paper with a KoBold author tested the planner only on synthetic problems. In May 2024, Caers wrote that the AI-planned campaign at Mingomba appraised the high-grade zone in about eight months. KoBold Africa chief executive Mfikeyi Makayi described the work at Mingomba in a first-person account in PwC’s October 2024 Zambia mining report. She reported that data science helped the team target areas with substantial copper grade and thickness. The work combined historical exploration, drilling, geoscience, and computing. She also described decades of exploration before KoBold entered the project. The sources therefore do not support a claim that AI first discovered the deposit. In April 2025, the International Energy Agency characterized the work as AI-assisted resource assessment. None of these accounts provides a controlled comparison or a quantified saving that is specific to AI. By March 2026 the project had moved into development, and Zambia's president launched shaft sinking on 29 April 2026.
purpose: The system supports geologists in choosing where to collect data and how to characterize mineral resources.
system: KoBold geological prediction and exploration systems
deployer: KoBold Metals and Mingomba Mining Limited
taxonomy_note: The benefit claim concerns resource characterization. Net climate gains, environmental savings, and a wholly new AI discovery are not established.

ratings.reason: Caers reports that the AI-planned campaign appraised the high-grade zone of the deposit in about eight months, and the project then moved into development. No source quantifies how much of this result the AI produced.

ai_role.statement: AI and data science contributed to a workflow that also used historical exploration data, drilling, and expert judgment. The separate contribution was not quantified.

evidence.citation: Jef Caers (Stanford University), The Mingomba high-grade copper discovery: where human intelligence meets artificial intelligence, The Mongolian Mining Journal, 29 May 2024. Caers co-developed the Intelligent Prospector drilling planner that he credits; he explains how historical drill data, unsupervised learning and thousands of geological models guided the choice of new drill holes, but he gives no comparison with a conventional campaign.
evidence.title: The Mingomba high-grade copper discovery: where human intelligence meets artificial intelligence
evidence.quote: Indeed, over the span of ~8 months of drilling the high-grade portion was confidently appraised.

evidence.citation: KoBold Metals, Mingomba project page, inspected 27 October 2026. The company describes the project as in development and distinguishes development from completed commercial production.
evidence.title: Mingomba

evidence.citation: John Mern and Jef Caers, The Intelligent Prospector v1.0: geoscientific model development and prediction by sequential data acquisition planning with application to mineral exploration, Geoscientific Model Development 16: 289-313, 11 January 2023. Mern lists KoBold Metals as his affiliation, and Caers later wrote that the planner helped characterize Mingomba; the paper tests the method only on synthetic two-dimensional problems and gives no Mingomba data.
evidence.title: The Intelligent Prospector v1.0: geoscientific model development and prediction by sequential data acquisition planning with application to mineral exploration
evidence.quote: Tests show that the proposed sequential approach is significantly more effective at reducing uncertainty than conventional methods.

evidence.citation: African Mining Market, Shaft-sinking project at Mingomba mine kicks off, 29 April 2026. The trade outlet has no stake in the project; it reports that President Hakainde Hichilema launched shaft sinking and quotes Zambian officials and KoBold's president, but it says nothing about the role of AI.
evidence.title: Shaft-sinking project at Mingomba mine kicks off
evidence.quote: has launched works to sink a 1.7 kilometres shaft at Mingomba Mine in Chililabombwe on the Copperbelt.

evidence.citation: African Mining Market, KoBold sets early-2030's first copper production at Mingomba project, 19 March 2026. The outlet reports KoBold's timeline and adds its own analysis that geology, power, smelting capacity and capital discipline will decide whether the project succeeds.
evidence.title: KoBold sets early-2030's first copper production at Mingomba project
evidence.quote: Whether it becomes a pillar of that goal will come down to geology, power, smelting capacity, and capital discipline.

fields.account: Jef Caers of Stanford University co-developed the Intelligent Prospector drilling planner. His 2023 paper with a KoBold author tested the planner only on synthetic problems. In May 2024, Caers wrote that the AI-planned campaign at Mingomba appraised the high-grade zone in about eight months. KoBold Africa chief executive Mfikeyi Makayi described the work at Mingomba in a first-person account in PwC’s October 2024 Zambia mining report. She reported that data science helped the team target areas with substantial copper grade and thickness. The work combined historical exploration, drilling, geoscience, and computing. She also described decades of exploration before KoBold entered the project. The sources therefore do not support a claim that AI first discovered the deposit. In April 2025, the International Energy Agency characterized the work as AI-assisted resource assessment. None of these accounts provides a controlled comparison or a quantified saving that is specific to AI. By March 2026 the project had moved into development, and Zambia's president launched shaft sinking on 29 April 2026.

produced_by: Historical information, new drilling, data science, and geologists’ decisions were combined.
must_hold: The reviewed sources do not establish causal conditions or an effect size for reproducing the benefit.
